To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the use of monoclonal antibody technology has led to the identification of new tumor-associated antigens and that the use of immunohistochemical techniques has been useful in the characterization of these antigens.

1) Monoclonal antibody reactivities are dependent on the form in which antigen is presented; 2) Monoclonals obtained after immunization of mice by the intraperitoneal route with aqueous cell extracts are likely to recognize cell surface antigens; 3) Monoclonally derived antibodies can recognize cell surface antigans, cell extracts and spent media; 4) Monoclonality can be confirmed by the use of a panel of hybridoma lines;
we have generated 600 monoclonal antibodies against the human prostate cancer cell lines PC-3 and DU-145.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of antigens on human prostate cancer cells and other tumor cells.
the development of monoclonal antibody-defined reagents for the detection and characterization of antigens associated with human prostate cancer.
the isolation and characterization of monoclonal and polyclonal antibodies which recognize cell surface antigens on human prostate cancer cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the antibodies described in this paper recognize molecules which are expressed on the surface of PC3 cells and are present in cell extracts and spent media.
the antibodies described here recognize a variety of antigens on human prostatic carcinoma, and that these antigens are not unique to this disease.

these monoclonal antibodies are not tumor-specific, and their use in the detection of prostate cancer would be limited to the immunohistologic detection of tumor cells in the presence of large numbers of normal cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the immunization of the mice with live cells resulted in the generation of antibodies with reactivity for live cells and spent culture media, whereas the immunization with cell extracts resulted in antibodies with reactivity only for cell extracts and spent media.
monoclonal antibodies have a great potential in the diagnosis of prostate cancer and in the study of the biology of the disease.
we have identified a variety of antigens that are expressed in prostate cancer and other cell lines.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the form of the antigen can have an impact on the resultant antibody and that immunohistochemistry can be used to test for reactivity.
immunization with live cancer cells can be used to generate antibodies with restricted reactivity for prostate carcinoma and other tumor types.
the form in which an antigen is presented can have a significant impact on the resulting specificity of a monoclonal antibody.
